20819.desc:
Satin is the fabric of ceremony, and a nightdress in satin borrows a little of that gravity even when the cut is pure bedroom. This one spends the loan on the back: a full backless line framed by angel-wing detailing at the shoulder blades, which is the element that turns a satin slip into a costume with a point of view.

The wings are the design's one flourish, and they are placed where the wearer cannot see them — which is deliberate costume logic. The front stays simple so the reveal happens when it turns. Satin gives the drape its weight and its light-catching surface; black and white versions split between nocturnal and bridal.

On the practical side, the same satin that looks ceremonial sleeps cooler than it gets credit for, and the piece doubles for occasions the listing photos are not subtle about: pajama evenings, wedding-adjacent events, dances.

20832.desc:
Jacquard weave makes its own pattern without a print — the design sits in the structure of the fabric, which is why it photographs the way it does under low light. On a cheongsam nightdress the effect is doubly useful: the silhouette supplies the tradition and the weave supplies the texture, with nothing printed on top to date either of them.

The cut runs to the standard cheongsam points — mandarin collar, diagonal front, fitted waist — and then adds the one flourish the style is famous for in lingerie form: a high slit at the leg. The slit is the moving part of the design; standing still this is a nightdress, walking it becomes something else.

Black and white versions of the same jacquard run in opposite directions — the black reads as evening, the white as boudoir morning — and both are polyester, which in jacquard means machine-washable texture.

The rundown:

  • Fabric: Polyester jacquard
  • Style: Cheongsam nightdress with high slit
  • Colors: Black, white
  • Fit: One size, recommended 40–60 kg (88–132 lbs)

Pattern woven in, slit cut in, nothing printed anywhere.

20837.desc:
A large bow on lingerie is costume logic: it frames the wearer as the present, and the size of the bow sets the size of the joke. This piece commits to a genuinely large one at the front of a black teddy — big enough to be the first thing noticed and the first thing untied — with the rest of the garment kept deliberately plain so the bow keeps the stage.

The teddy underneath is a one-piece jumpsuit cut in polyester, fitted through the body and closing at the crotch. Black was the right call for the palette: a bow this size in any other color would read as costume-party, in black it reads as intentional.

As a gift the piece does half the wrapping on its own; as a self-purchase it makes an occasion out of an ordinary evening, which is the entire economic argument for lingerie.

20852.desc:
Two openings named in the title tell most of the story of this jumpsuit: an open cup at the bust and an open crotch at the base, with sheer black mesh lace doing what remains. It is a design that has stopped negotiating with the concept of a garment and started editing it directly.

What holds the piece together is the lace itself — a stretch mesh with enough pattern density to read as clothing from across a room and enough openness to abandon the claim up close. The shoulders and hips carry the structure so the two open sections stay where they are put rather than wandering with movement.

One size covers the standard weight band, and the stretch lace does the fitting. There is nothing to fasten, nothing to untie, and nothing between the design's premise and its execution.

20857.desc:
Denim styling translated into lingerie fabric is a specific trick: the cues — the wash, the cut, the pocket lines — say one thing while the material says another. These shorts run the routine faithfully in polyester, cut short and fitted, with a denim-look finish that survives the translation because the silhouette is doing the recalling.

The appeal is the reversal. Denim is the fabric of ordinary days; these are shorts for a night that is anything but, and the gap between the reference and the use is the whole point. Worn with a plain top they read as a denim cutoff; worn as intended they stop pretending halfway.

Three graded sizes rather than one, because a fitted short is the one garment where the weight band matters most — M covers 40–50 kg, L 50–60 kg, and XL 60–70 kg.

A uniform reference in chiffon is the softer version of the genre: the same borrowed authority as leather, but delivered in a fabric that apologizes for nothing because it whispers. This one-piece keeps the uniform cues at the collar and front line, then lets chiffon take the rest of the design where it wants to go.

The fit runs wide by intent — a single size covering 40–70 kg, with the drape rather than the stretch doing the adjusting. That width is what makes the piece read as lingerie rather than as shrunken daywear: chiffon needs air between it and the body to do its work, and this cut provides it.

As sleepwear it is light enough to forget about; as anything else it is a costume that travels flat and washes cold. The two jobs do not compete.

Skinny cuts in patent leather leave nowhere for the fit to hide: the gloss shows every seam decision, and a cut this close makes them all in public. This teddy makes its choices early — a high leg line, a plain neckline, and a body that maps rather than skims — and executes them without the safety net of stretch-knit forgiveness.

Styling runs minimal by default: this is a piece that expects to be the entire outfit, and adding to it usually subtracts. Heels, if anything, and only when the floor demands them.

As a nightdress it functions: lace at this weight breathes, the straps stay put, and the cut is generous enough to sleep in without rearranging. As anything else it functions better, which is the standard bargain of the genre and the reason the sheer end of the scale exists.

The color follows the listing photos. One size covers the 40–60 kg band with the lace doing the fitting, and there is nothing on the piece to adjust, fasten, or negotiate with — the design is one decision, seen through.

In sheer lace with a loose nightdress line through the body, it spends the evening as sleepwear until the moment it does not — and the open crotch is what removes the transition.

The lace is openwork rather than solid mesh, which keeps the jumpsuit light and makes the nightdress reading credible. One size covers the 40–60 kg band, the straps are the only adjustable element, and the pull-on construction means the entire fastening inventory is zero.

This is the version of the open-crotch design for people who want the feature without the architecture — no hardware, no strapping, nothing that announces itself until it is relevant.

20993.desc:

This nightdress mounts one at the bust of a sheer lace slip, sized honestly rather than apologetically, and lets that single gesture carry the design — the rest of the piece is deliberately quiet.

The lace body runs sheer with a steady openwork repeat, cut straight from a high bust line to a mid-thigh hem. The bow sits where the eye lands first and does double duty as the focal point and as the one piece of the garment with any structure to it.

Practically, it is a slip first: light enough to sleep in, simple enough to wash cold, and generous in the one-size band of 40–60 kg. What happens after the bow is undone is outside the product specification.
